messages.content: You are a English writing tutor. You help writers make their posts say what they mean, for the people who will read them.

Target language: English. The writer's own language: Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China).
Where it will be posted: Reddit question post. Who will read it: Warrior Cats fans who know Darktail's Judgment. What the writer wants to do: Ask about StarClan's silence at the moonstone and share their view.
The writer's note about it, in their words: r/WarriorCats 的提问帖。我刚开始读 Darktail’s Judgment，想问 Darkpaw 在月亮石那一段，还想说说我的看法。
The writer's draft. A separate pass fixes its small language errors (grammar, articles, tense, wrong words); ignore those. Passages in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) are things the writer could not yet say; "a/b" marks a choice they have not made. Sentences are numbered:
[S1] I’m on the early chapters of Darktail’s Judgment, and I get a little bit confused about the plot that StarClan didn’t show up when Darkpaw was at the moonstone and he went really miserable and furious for that.

[S2] Ravenpaw said StarClan had travelled with the Clans and left the forest skies, and it would be hard / not worth it to get back here for a distant little kittypet who want to join the Clans.
[S3] But it was mentioned in the book that it was a overcast day, so without the moonlight it’s natural to be unable to reach StarClan back then when the Clans were still in the forest.
[S4] (Could someone tell me if there was a similar case in the other books that the night sky’s cloudy when some cat’s at the Moonstone?
[S5] Or do StarClan have the power to clear the clouds if they want to communicate?)

[S6] And Darkpaw didn’t go for another try on a clear day; he just chose to transform himself into Darktail👿 instead.
The first pass left these words as the writer wrote them, because fixing them needs something only the writer can decide; each must be inside one of your spots: «hard / not worth it».

A fluent writer's version of the same post, for comparison (not to be copied wholesale):
<<<
Just started Darktail's Judgment and I'm kinda lost on why StarClan never showed up for Darkpaw at the moonstone 😩 he was so miserable and furious about it, and I get why lol

Ravenpaw says StarClan went travelling with the Clans and left the forest skies, so it'd be too much trouble to come back just for some random kittypet who wanted to join. BUT the book also says it was overcast that day, so no moonlight, and that would explain why they couldn't reach StarClan back when the Clans were still in the forest. Has anyone seen another moonstone scene where the sky was cloudy? Or can StarClan clear the clouds if they really want to talk? ~

And Darkpaw never tried again on a clear night, he just went and turned himself into Darktail 👿
>>>

Small language errors are handled separately. Now find every place worth a second pass. There are two kinds of spot.

kind "meaning": the post cannot do its job until the writer decides something only they know:
- passages still in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) that are whole clauses (the writer will build them in English themselves), and "a/b" choices;
- a point the reader needs but the post leaves unstated (a conclusion the evidence is meant to support, the actual question);
- a connective or framing word whose relation (contrast, concession, cause, addition) does not match the ideas it joins, or whose other half never comes;
- wording that readers could take another way than the writer means, as defined below;
- wording off in register, as defined below: read as meant, but not how to speak to these readers.

kind "formulation": the meaning comes through, but a fluent writer would package it differently, and the difference is worth learning: the order of information, where the emphasis falls, a comparison that is not like for like, chains of nouns where English would use a verb or a clause, an image, joke or set phrase carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) that a English reader would take literally or not recognise, praise or criticism framed from an angle this community would not use, quoted or reported words not built into the sentence, a sentence or passage carrying too much at once. Compare each sentence with the fluent version above: where that version is built differently (not just a word swapped), decide whether the difference teaches something. List every such place; the writer will skip what they do not want. Word-level fixes with one obvious answer are not spots.

Words are taken another way than meant when a reader, reaching them, would come away with a different
- attitude or feeling: praise heard as a complaint, impatience or sarcasm; warmth as coldness; a joke as an insult; criticism heard as much harsher or milder than meant;
- act: a wish or hope heard as a demand, a question as a claim, news as a request, or the reverse;
- claim: who did what, what happened, what the writer thinks or knows (for example, that they misunderstood the work);
- strength: far stronger or weaker than meant (mild surprise heard as shock, a small doubt as rejection, liking as indifference).
It counts even when the rest of the post lets a careful reader work the intent out afterwards: words are read before what follows them, and a reader who first feels criticised, pushed or misjudged has been misread, however briefly (a friend told "you've really changed" hears a reproach before the next sentence makes it a compliment). It does not count when the difference would not change how the reader feels about the post or how they would answer: a shade of tone, a synonym, words that readers of this community take exactly as meant.

Words are off in register when they are read as meant but do not suit who is speaking to whom here, by the writer's relationship to the readers and this community's manners: too demanding or pushy (a reader telling an author what to do or how fast to write; a student giving a professor a deadline), too blunt or curt, too familiar, or too stiff and formal for the place, or presuming what is not theirs to decide (unasked criticism, telling an author what their characters should do). It counts even when some people here write that way: what matters is how the one addressed feels on receiving it (pressured, talked down to, put off, kept at a distance). Casual style that this place expects is not off in register.

Skip anything that is a matter of taste only. One spot per problem: two problems in neighbouring sentences are two spots.

A figure the writer made on purpose (a parallel or echo that turns the same word on something new, a deliberate repetition, wordplay) is judged by its words. If they are what a fluent writer would use, it is the writer's voice and never a spot by itself. If a word in it is not (a English reader would stop at it), that word is a spot like any other, and its problem says both that the figure works and why that word does not.

For each spot, in this order:
- kind.
- quote: the exact words of the draft where a reader first stumbles, copied character for character: a few words inside one sentence.
- problem: in English, as the tutor who just read it, one or two sentences: starting from the quoted words, what a English reader expects or understands on reaching them and why (what those words normally do in English), and what is then missing, off or hard to follow. Specific to these words; never the fix or the better wording, which the writer will find themselves.
- scope: what the writer will rewrite, the smallest unit the problem and their decision affect: "words" (only the quoted words), "sentence" (the sentence containing them) or "sentences" (several neighbouring sentences, for a passage that carries too much or is ordered badly; list them in sentences).
- sentences: the numbers of the sentences the scope covers.
- question: the one thing the writer must tell you about what they mean here, as a short English question.
- mode and readings: what the writer might mean, in English. Readings must be genuinely different meanings that would be written differently in English; if there is no second reading like that, give one. mode "one" when one reading is clearly the likeliest (put it first); mode "ask" when the writer must choose. A reading's label is that reading in a few words (about six Chinese characters or three words), what the writer taps to say "this one"; never a letter or a number.

Also give the post's argument map: the steps of what the post does, in order, each pointing at its sentences, status "missing" (with sentences []) for a step the reader needs but the post leaves out, "fix" for a step that is there but does not work yet. role is a label that fits in about six Chinese characters or twelve Latin letters (one to three short words); what says the step in at most about twelve words; note, only for fix and missing, says in one short sentence what is wrong.

All writer-facing text (gist, role, what, note, problem, question, readings) in English, short.

Work in two steps.

Step 1. Under "### ARGUMENT", write out in plain prose what this writer is trying to get across, step by step, including the steps and the real question they leave implicit. Then say, for each step, whether a reader who has only the post would get it.

Step 2. Under "### JSON", give the analysis:
First fill scan: one row for every numbered sentence, in order, with the matching words from the fluent version and whether it is built the same (none), differs only in words (word), or is built differently (structure). Every structure row must then be judged for a formulation spot.
{"scan":[{"s":1,"fluent":"the words in the fluent version that say what sentence 1 says","differs":"none|word|structure"}],"gist":"what the post is really asking or saying","map":[{"role":"...","what":"...","sentences":[1],"status":"ok|fix|missing","note":"..."}],"spots":[{"kind":"meaning|formulation","quote":"exact words","problem":"...","scope":"words|sentence|sentences","sentences":[1],"question":"...","mode":"one|ask","readings":[{"label":"...","meaning":"..."}]}]}

result.text:
### ARGUMENT

The writer is asking why StarClan did not answer Darkpaw at the Moonstone, when he was miserable and furious about it. Ravenpaw's explanation in the book is that StarClan had travelled with the Clans and left the forest skies, so coming back for one unimportant kittypet would not be worth the trouble (or would be hard). The writer pushes back with a second explanation from the book: the day was overcast, so there was no moonlight, which would explain why the Clans could not reach StarClan then. The writer then asks the community two things: whether any other book has a cloudy Moonstone scene, and whether StarClan can clear clouds when they want to communicate. The post ends by noting that Darkpaw never retried on a clear night and turned himself into Darktail instead. The implicit question is: is the silence a plot hole, or does the overcast sky explain it?

For each step:
- Step 1, the question (why StarClan stayed silent): a reader can follow it, but "confused about the plot that..." makes the question hard to find, so the reader may not know what is being asked. Partly gets through.
- Step 2, Ravenpaw's explanation: a reader gets it. The choice between "hard" and "not worth it" is unresolved, so the reader cannot tell which reason is being reported. Partly gets through.
- Step 3, the overcast counter-explanation: a reader gets the content, but it reads more as a report of the book than the writer's own view, and "it's natural to be unable" is awkward. Partly gets through.
- Step 4, the community questions: a reader gets them, apart from a clumsy "that the night sky's cloudy". Gets through.
- Step 5, the retry point: a reader cannot see what it is for. "Clear day" also suggests a misunderstanding of how the Moonstone works. Does not get through yet.
